Impressed that Vue 3 redesigned both its internal architecture and public API while keeping users happy, instead of falling into the trap of fitting contemporary practices and becoming less relevant as the ecosystem changes.

Vue's reactivity API for component state, effects and computed values is more ergonomic than React's. But defining many small components is harder with Single-File Components, so they use Vue with TSX. That is 'okay' and 'totally usable' but not as solid as React, because almost nobody in the Vue community uses JSX/TSX.

Hoped for better TypeScript support for typing props, where 90% of their type errors occur. You still have to declare prop types manually with PropType casts rather than a plain interface as in React. 'I would recommend still avoiding Vue for this reason alone.'
Vue is the only one of the top three frameworks that can easily be added minimally here and there to existing templates to spruce up old applications. Gradual adoption is a real selling point.
Seeing code like $childRef.setData({...}), where a parent sets a child's data, in a Vue codebase hurt their head. They still prefer React for its consistent reasoning about data flow.

Used React for years but disliked JSX. Single-file components separating HTML, JS and styles won them over. They've used Vue for all new projects since and feel it has everything React has, in a more polished, thought-out way.
Tried Vue first, then moved to React because it clicked better and had more/better libraries: 'Nothing on the Vue side of things is as good as Material UI.'

Built semi-large apps in both and prefers React. Vue is intuitive, like a light-weight Angular 1, but two-way binding caused confusion about where state lives and implicit state changes. Single-file components are the best part. The template DSL is the biggest problem: complicated tree renders are hard compared with plain JS in JSX.

Team moved from React to Vue ~8 months ago and everyone is happier. Reasons: they hated JSX and its boilerplate, and Vue has an official router and store (Vuex), which beats Redux with Vue's reactivity. The docs, both technical and narrative guides, are among the best they've used. 'We would never go back to React.'

Killer features keeping them on React: React Native (Weex not production ready), streaming SSR, Relay, JSX by default rather than Vue's Angular-esque template language with new syntax and directives, and corporate backing.

Backend dev chose Vue for a real-time SignalR debug UI because it used plain objects, so server data could be passed in directly. Months later they picked it back up nearly instantly and made substantial changes, unlike their Ember app. 'You can learn the basics of Vue in minutes, and be quite adept within hours.'

Veteran of jQuery, Backbone, Angular, Ember and React in production: Vue 2 with single-file components is what everyone looks for. Benefits: fast, a learning curve of hours, CLI scaffolding, simple .vue files without JSX, and official routing and state packages. Vuex 2 is one of the cleanest flux implementations they've seen.

Great for side projects. With React they struggled to choose and track libraries and hated configuring webpack. Vue's official vuex and vue-router, plus vue-cli scaffolding, make it easy to iterate on prototypes via single-file components with scoped CSS.

Hates that Vue's reactivity system only tracks changes under certain conditions. Uses Vue mainly for lightweight apps because state management pushes all logic into Vuex. Finds Laracasts good for help on obscure problems.

Built their SPA with Vue and very pleased. Most stumbling blocks were solved via the guide, GitHub issues and the forum. Uses Nuxt.js for SSR, which works great. Recommends Vue for anyone building their first SPA: easy to pick up.

Spends days building an app, then days getting Vue's build tooling configured, googling from one unclear error to another. Likes Vue's strengths but is ready to ditch it over 'complete and utter garbage' build/debug configuration.

Adopted Vue 2 years ago and extremely happy: easy to get into, gentle learning curve, just works. But TypeScript support is mediocre and clearly second class, there are no accepted best practices (e.g. where API calls go), and third-party component design varies wildly.

Used React full-time and tried Vue for a personal IDE-like project; Vue felt like a 'breath of fresh air' at first. They converted back to React because they needed more control. Vue is a jQuery successor for websites but too 'magical' for really complex apps.
Passing data back to parents in Vue is awkward: emit requires explicitly re-emitting up each level, while Vuex as a global ties components to it and breaks modularity.
Vuetify, Vue's material design component set, is 'way better built' than Angular's material component set, based on using both.
